title: Turning audio into speech features · Level 3
slo: Describe how a speech recognition system captures and prepares audio.

exercises.question_text: How long is an MFCC audio frame commonly?

options.rationale: MFCC extraction splits audio into overlapping windows of about 20–30 milliseconds. These short frames are the units used for frequency analysis.

options.error_type: Confuses frame duration with sampling rate
options.rationale: 8–16 kHz is a common speech sampling-rate range. It measures samples per second rather than frame length.
options.better_fit: Choose this when choosing a common speech sampling rate.

feedback.intrinsic: The frame duration would be confused with the rate used to record audio.
feedback.instructional: Milliseconds describe frame length. Kilohertz describes how many samples are taken each second.

options.rationale: Thirteen is a common number of coefficients in one MFCC vector. It is not a duration, and MFCC frames are measured in milliseconds.
options.better_fit: Choose 13 when describing coefficient values in one feature vector.

feedback.intrinsic: Audio would be grouped into frames far longer than intended.
feedback.instructional: One frame is about 20–30 milliseconds; one vector often has 13 coefficient values.

options.error_type: Confuses music sampling rate with frame duration
options.rationale: 44.1 kHz is a music sampling rate, not a 44.1-millisecond frame duration. MFCC frames are commonly about 20–30 milliseconds.
options.better_fit: Choose 44.1 kHz when discussing higher-detail music capture.

feedback.intrinsic: The timing of feature extraction would be based on a different measurement.
feedback.instructional: Do not mix kilohertz with milliseconds. MFCC frames use short 20–30 ms windows.

exercises.explanation: Correct. MFCC extraction commonly analyzes overlapping audio frames of about 20–30 milliseconds.

exercises.question_text: Which facts about sampling rates are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A higher sampling rate takes more measurements each second. This captures more audio detail.
More measurements create more information to process. Higher rates therefore require more processing.

options.text: 44.1 kHz is a typical music rate.
options.rationale: 44.1 kHz is a higher rate commonly used for music. It captures more detail than common speech rates.

options.text: Higher rates remove all background noise.
options.rationale: Higher sampling rates capture more detail, but they do not remove all noise. Filters may reduce hums, clicks, or background noise.
options.better_fit: Choose noise filtering when unwanted recorded sound needs to be reduced.

feedback.intrinsic: A noisy call could still be hard to recognize despite using a higher rate.
feedback.instructional: Rate affects captured detail and processing needs; filtering addresses unwanted sound.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Higher rates capture more detail and require more processing; 44.1 kHz is a typical music rate.

exercises.question_text: Sampling rate is the number of audio measurements taken each second.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The recording settings would be described incorrectly, making rate choices harder to compare.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Sampling rate counts the measurements taken each second, such as 16,000 per second for 16 kHz.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Sampling rate tells how many numeric audio measurements are taken each second.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe the Mel scale? Select all that apply.

options.text: It adjusts frequency bins for human hearing.
options.rationale: The Mel scale adjusts frequency bins to match human hearing sensitivity. This makes the representation emphasize perceptually important frequency ranges.
People distinguish low pitches better than high pitches. The Mel scale reflects this difference in hearing sensitivity.

options.text: It is used after frequency analysis.
options.rationale: MFCC extraction first applies a Fourier transform to reveal frequencies. It then maps those frequency bins to the Mel scale.

options.error_type: Confuses Mel mapping with linguistic analysis
options.rationale: Text-to-phoneme conversion occurs during linguistic analysis in speech synthesis. Mel mapping adjusts frequencies from an audio frame during recognition feature extraction.
options.better_fit: Choose this for linguistic analysis, which maps written letters and words to phonemes.

feedback.intrinsic: Written pronunciation work would be confused with audio feature preparation.
feedback.instructional: The Mel scale works with frequencies from audio. Linguistic analysis works with written text and phonemes.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The Mel scale follows frequency analysis and adjusts frequency bins to reflect human hearing, especially finer low-pitch distinction.

exercises.question_text: What range commonly balances clarity and efficiency for speech recognition?

options.rationale: Speech recognition commonly balances clarity and efficiency at about 8–16 kHz. This range needs less processing than a higher music rate while retaining useful speech clarity.

options.error_type: Confuses sampling rate with frame duration
options.rationale: 20–30 milliseconds describes the length of an MFCC audio frame. It is a duration, not a number of samples per second.
options.better_fit: Choose this when describing how audio is divided during MFCC extraction.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would set a frame length when it needed to choose a recording rate.
feedback.instructional: kHz measures samples per second. Milliseconds measure the duration of one audio frame.

options.error_type: Confuses rate with MFCC vector size
options.rationale: Thirteen is a common number of values in one MFCC feature vector. It does not describe sampling rate.
options.better_fit: Choose this when describing the usual size of one MFCC vector for a frame.

feedback.intrinsic: The recording would have no meaningful rate setting from this number.
feedback.instructional: A sampling rate is measured in kHz; coefficients summarize an already prepared frame.

options.error_type: Confuses music detail with common speech balance
options.rationale: 44.1 kHz captures more detail and is typical for music. It also requires more processing than the common speech balance.
options.better_fit: Choose this when extra music detail is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: A basic voice-command feature could use more processing than necessary.
feedback.instructional: For common speech recognition, about 8–16 kHz balances clarity and efficiency.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Speech commonly uses about 8–16 kHz to balance clarity with efficient processing.

exercises.question_text: MFCC extraction divides a recording into ___ frames so adjacent frames share some audio.

parts.text: MFCC extraction divides a recording into
frames so adjacent frames share some audio.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The framing method for feature extraction would be stated incorrectly.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use overlapping. MFCC extraction analyzes overlapping short frames rather than completely separate frames.

exercises.explanation: MFCC extraction uses overlapping frames, meaning adjacent frames share some audio samples. The frames are then analyzed as short time segments.

exercises.question_text: A higher sampling rate captures more detail while requiring less processing.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A team might underestimate the processing needed for higher-quality audio.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The trade-off goes together: more samples per second capture more detail and create more processing work.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Higher sampling rates provide more detail, and that extra detail requires more processing.

exercises.question_text: A common speech sampling rate is 16,000 samples per second, also called ___.

parts.text: A common speech sampling rate is 16,000 samples per second, also called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The recording rate would remain unclear when configuring voice input.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use 16 kHz for 16,000 measurements per second. MFCCs and mel-spectrograms are audio representations, not sampling rates.

exercises.explanation: The prefix kilo means one thousand, so 16,000 measurements each second is 16 kHz. This is a common speech sampling rate.

exercises.question_text: What does a Fourier transform reveal in an audio frame?

options.rationale: A Fourier transform changes an audio frame from the time domain to the frequency domain. This reveals which pitches are present in that frame.
Written words are selected later during decoding. Fourier analysis reveals frequency content, not a transcription.
options.better_fit: Choose this for decoding, which selects the best word sequence.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would mistake sound-frequency information for a finished transcript.
feedback.instructional: Fourier analysis identifies pitches. Decoding combines later predictions to select words.

options.error_type: Confuses audio conditions with frequency analysis
options.rationale: Distance from the speaker affects downstream accuracy, but a Fourier transform does not identify microphone distance. It reveals pitches in an audio frame.
options.better_fit: Choose microphone distance when evaluating audio-quality conditions that affect recognition accuracy.

feedback.intrinsic: A recording issue could be confused with the analysis performed on its frames.
feedback.instructional: Keep audio conditions separate from frequency analysis. Fourier transforms reveal pitches.

options.rationale: The final audio waveform is generated during speech synthesis by a neural vocoder. A Fourier transform analyzes an existing frame rather than generating audio.
options.better_fit: Choose this for the output of speech synthesis after vocoding.

feedback.intrinsic: The analysis step would be mistaken for the stage that creates spoken output.
feedback.instructional: Fourier transforms inspect frequency content; neural vocoders generate audio waveforms.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A Fourier transform reveals the pitches present by changing a frame into frequency information.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about MFCCs are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: They are a common speech feature representation.
options.rationale: MFCCs are a common feature extraction representation in speech recognition. They provide compact vectors for later acoustic modeling.
MFCCs use the Mel scale to emphasize frequency ranges important to human hearing. Less important ranges are compressed.
MFCC coefficients summarize the spectral shape of each short audio frame. A small set of values represents useful sound characteristics.

options.text: They are final spoken audio samples.
options.rationale: MFCCs are feature values derived from captured audio. Final spoken audio is a waveform produced during synthesis.
options.better_fit: Choose this for raw audio waveform values created during speech synthesis.

feedback.intrinsic: A learner might treat compact features as audio that a listener could hear.
feedback.instructional: MFCCs describe short frames for recognition. They are not the final audible waveform.

exercises.explanation: Correct. MFCCs are compact speech features that reflect hearing-important frequencies and spectral shape.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The purpose of Mel mapping could be unclear when explaining MFCC preparation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Name the Mel scale first, then state that it adjusts frequency bins to reflect human hearing sensitivity.

exercises.correct_answer: The Mel scale adjusts frequency bins to reflect human hearing sensitivity
exercises.explanation: The order identifies the Mel scale, its action on frequency bins, and the reason for that action. It aligns audio features with human hearing sensitivity.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The purpose of MFCC features would be described unclearly.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Begin with MFCCs, then state that they summarize spectral shape of short frames for recognition.

exercises.correct_answer: MFCCs summarize spectral shape of short frames for recognition
exercises.explanation: MFCCs provide a compact summary of the spectral shape within short audio frames. This representation supports efficient speech recognition.
